implementation_notes: foreach is the enumeration message: the compiler calls GetEnumerator() - pattern-based, so any type with a public GetEnumerator returning something with Current and MoveNext() works without implementing IEnumerable<T> - and runs the body for each element, handling IDisposable enumerators for you. Since C# 3 the same protocol is wrapped by the LINQ operators (Enumerable.Select/Where/Sum/Aggregate), which return lazily evaluated IEnumerable<T> sequences, so enumeration becomes the terminal step (foreach, ToList, Count). The classic index loop survives for position-dependent walks (parallel arrays, ring buffers) and for hot loops where the enumerator allocation matters.
pitfalls: LINQ is deferred: nothing runs until the sequence is enumerated, so exceptions surface at the foreach (not at the query) and re-enumerating re-executes any captured side effects.

List<T>.ForEach(Action<T>) and Enumerable.ToList().ForEach(...) cannot break or return a value and allocate a delegate per call; use a foreach loop or a query for anything beyond a terminal side effect.
Modifying the source collection during iteration throws InvalidOperationException, and a captured variable reused after the loop observes the last element.

variants.name: LINQ query composition
variants.idiom_name: Enumerable.Select/Where/Sum composed with lambdas (or query syntax)
variants.implementation_notes: C# 3 turns the transforming enumeration messages into extension methods: Where/Select/Sum/Aggregate (or the equivalent query syntax the compiler rewrites into those calls) express collect/select/inject directly, and the walk happens only at the terminal step. Prefer it when enumeration produces a value; keep the foreach form when the body performs side effects, because a deferred query makes execution order and exception timing surprising.
variants.code_sketch:
var bySku = order.Lines
    .Where(l => l.IsTaxable)
    .GroupBy(l => l.Sku)
    .Select(g => new { g.Key, Total = g.Sum(l => l.Amount) });
foreach (var row in bySku) Report(row.Key, row.Total);  // walk starts here
pitfalls: Because the query is deferred, a captured variable read inside it sees the value at enumeration time, not at query-definition time - a classic offline bug when the query outlives the loop that built it.
GroupBy and OrderBy buffer the whole sequence before yielding, so chaining them converts a streaming walk into a materialising one.
